**Table 7.5.** Effects of clays and shales on logging measurements.

| Measurement | Effect |
|---|---|
| Spontaneous potential, SP | SP is decreased in magnitude with respect to the shale baseline. |
| Gamma ray | Increased radioactivity is apparent as less movement away from the nearby shale values than an equivalent clean sand. |
| Sonic | Sonic porosity is higher than the actual formation porosity due to the higher travel time of the clays/shales. |
| Neutron | Neutron porosity is higher than the actual formation porosity due to the water that is part of the clay structure and is adsorbed on the clay surfaces. |
| Density | Density porosity is higher than the actual formation porosity due to the generally lower matrix densities of most clay minerals. If the matrix density of the clay is close to that of the formation matrix, there is little or no effect on porosity. |
| Resistivity | Resistivity is less than that in an equivalent clean formation due to the conductivity of the clay. This produces a calculated water saturation greater than the actual formation water saturation. (Archie's equation assumes that all conductivity is from the formation water and that the formation matrix is completely nonconducting.) |

figures.description: Flowchart for scanning logs to identify zones of interest (both pay and wet), with two parallel paths. Top box: 'Look for clean zones' (footnote 1) branches to 'Clastics' (left) and 'Carbonates' (right). Clastics path: 'Look for resistivity' (footnote 2) → LOW leads to 'Water zone — Use as baseline (wet) comparison'; HIGH leads to 'Check porosity' → LOW gives 'Tight. Unlikely pay.'; HIGH gives 'Zone of interest'. Carbonates path: 'Look for porosity' → LOW gives 'Tight. Unlikely pay.'; HIGH leads to 'Check resistivity' → LOW gives 'Water zone — Use as baseline (wet) comparison'; HIGH gives 'Zone of interest'. Both 'Zone of interest' boxes feed 'Begin detailed analysis'. Footnotes: 1 Zones that appear to be shales might be radioactive productive zones. 2 Shaly zones might produce oil or gas even if they have low resistivity. Accompanying text: for clastics the resistivity log is the primary reconnaissance measurement because clastics tend to consist of reservoirs surrounded by shales whose resistivities vary gradually with depth, so fluid-content differences make reservoir resistivities stand out against relatively constant shale resistivity. For carbonates, formation resistivities vary widely with changing rock types and few shales exist as reference, so the porosity log is the primary reconnaissance measurement; finding porous zones identifies zones with capacity to hold fluids. Combining this scanning technique with the neutron-density quick-look technique of Chapter 4 allows identification of lithology (and sometimes fluid type).

Caption text: 'Example of the generalized lithologic response of the neutron and density logs, used as a quick-look lithology technique. The gamma ray (GR) and photoelectric effect (PEF) are provided for additional information. Procedure: The neutron-porosity and density-porosity curves are scanned for their relationship to each other and for their values. The relative position of the curves is an indicator of the lithology encountered, and the average of the two curves at any depth is a good approximation of the porosity (within two porosity units). The gamma ray may be used to distinguish ambiguous patterns, like shale and dolomite patterns. The photoelectric effect may be used to distinguish ambiguous patterns (sandy limestone from dolomitic sand) or to confirm the neutron-density interpretation. Assumptions: There is liquid in the pore space, either water or oil but not gas. The formations encountered do not contain clay (except for the shale). Both porosity curves are referenced to limestone. Note the lithology interpretations listed on the log.'
